q: An auditor selects every 40th voucher after a random start from a population of 8000 payment vouchers. Under SA 530 this selection is best described as:
o: Systematic selection, which can be statistical where the start is random
Non-statistical selection, because judgement fixed the interval width
Monetary unit sampling, because a constant interval is being applied
Haphazard selection, because no selection probability is ever computed
why: Systematic selection with a random start gives each item a known chance of selection, so it qualifies for statistical sampling, provided the population has no structure that coincides with the sampling interval. MUS also uses an interval, but the interval runs over monetary units, not physical items.

q: Which of the following is a consequence of sampling risk rather than non-sampling risk?
o: The auditor applies an unsuitable audit procedure to the items selected
The auditor misses a misstatement in an item that was actually examined
The auditor concludes a control works when the true rate exceeds tolerable
A team member misreads a confirmation reply received from a trade customer
why: Sampling risk is the risk that the conclusion from the sample differs from the conclusion had the entire population been tested, which is exactly the risk of incorrectly accepting effective controls. Applying wrong procedures or missing a misstatement in an item actually examined are non-sampling risks and are not reduced by increasing sample size.

q: In monetary unit sampling for a trade receivables balance, which population item is CERTAIN to be selected?
o: Any item whose book value equals the population average book value
Any item carrying a negative or credit book value at the period end
Any item that was also selected in the prior year audit sample
Any item whose book value equals or exceeds the sampling interval used
why: In MUS each rupee is a sampling unit, so an item at least as large as the interval must contain at least one selected monetary unit and is picked with certainty. Negative balances are actually a known weakness of MUS and must be tested separately, not automatically included.

q: An auditor sets tolerable misstatement at 60 percent of performance materiality for a substantive sample. Increasing tolerable misstatement while all else is unchanged will:
o: Increase the sample size, since more precision is demanded
Decrease the sample size, since less precision is demanded
Leave sample size unchanged, but raise the sampling risk faced
Force the auditor to move from non-statistical to statistical sampling
why: Sample size varies inversely with tolerable misstatement, because a larger amount the auditor is willing to accept demands less precision. The tempting answer is that a bigger tolerance means more work, but the relationship is the opposite.

q: SA 530 permits the auditor to treat a misstatement as an anomaly only when:
o: It arose from a one-off cause and is demonstrably not representative
It falls below the performance materiality set for the engagement
Management has agreed to correct the misstatement in full before signing
It arose from a control deviation rather than a recording error
why: An anomaly requires a high degree of certainty, supported by additional procedures, that the item is demonstrably not representative of the population. Size and management correction are irrelevant to whether the cause could recur elsewhere in the population.

q: Stratification of an accounts receivable population by balance size primarily achieves which of the following?
o: Elimination of non-sampling risk within each of the strata formed
Conversion of a non-statistical approach into a statistical one
Removal of the need to project misstatements in the low value stratum
Reduction of variability within strata, allowing a smaller sample
why: Stratification groups items with similar characteristics so that variability within each stratum falls, which reduces the total sample size needed. Misstatements found in a stratum still have to be projected to that stratum, and stratification does nothing about non-sampling risk.

q: An auditor tests 60 items from a population of 12000 purchase orders and finds 3 without required approval. The tolerable deviation rate is 5 percent. The most appropriate immediate conclusion is:
o: The deviation rate of 5 percent equals tolerable, so the control is effective
The three exceptions are anomalies and should be excluded from the results
The rate of 5 percent leaves no allowance for sampling risk, so no reliance
The sample should be extended to 120 items and the two rates averaged
why: A sample deviation rate equal to the tolerable rate leaves no room for the allowance for sampling risk, so the upper deviation rate exceeds tolerable and reliance is not supported. Treating deviations as anomalies requires demonstrated non-representativeness, which is not established here.

q: Which factor would MOST reduce the required sample size in a test of details of a large inventory balance?
o: A rise in the assessed risk of material misstatement for the balance
A fall in the misstatement the auditor expects in the population
Stratifying the population into fewer and considerably wider strata
A rise in the number of items in the population from 50000 to 90000
why: Lower expected misstatement means less allowance is needed and sample size falls. Population size has almost no effect on sample size for large populations, which is a common misconception, and higher assessed risk increases sample size.

q: After projecting the misstatement from a substantive sample, the projected misstatement is below performance materiality but close to it. Under SA 530 the auditor should:
o: Conclude the population is not materially misstated because projection is lower
Reduce performance materiality so that the projection falls comfortably within it
Ask management to record the full projected misstatement as an audit adjustment
Consider that projection plus sampling risk may exceed tolerable, and extend
why: The evaluation must compare projected misstatement plus the allowance for sampling risk against tolerable misstatement, so a projection close to the threshold means the population may still be materially misstated. Lowering materiality after the fact to fit the result reverses the required logic.

q: Which statement about projecting misstatements is correct under SA 530?
o: Misstatements in items tested 100 percent are added in full, not projected
Anomalies are projected but carry a reduced weighting in the estimate
Misstatements in items tested in full are projected to the remainder
Only understatements are projected, since overstatements get corrected first
why: Items tested in full are not part of the sampled remainder, so misstatements in them are known misstatements added in full rather than projected. Projecting them would double count and overstate the estimated misstatement.

q: An auditor plans a test of controls over authorisation of journal entries and expects zero deviations. Which change would MOST increase the sample size?
o: Raising the tolerable deviation rate from 5 percent to 8 percent
Reducing the desired confidence level from 95 percent to 90 percent
Raising the expected deviation rate from 0 percent to 2 percent
Raising the population from 4000 to 9000 authorised journal entries
why: When the expected deviation rate moves closer to the tolerable rate, the required sample size rises sharply. Raising tolerable rate and lowering confidence both shrink the sample, and population size is largely irrelevant for large populations.

q: Which approach does NOT constitute audit sampling as defined in SA 530?
o: Selecting 45 items from 3000 invoices using random number tables
Selecting every item above a stated amount and testing only those
Selecting 30 items haphazardly, each item having a chance of selection
Selecting every 25th shipping document after a random starting point
why: Audit sampling requires all items in the population to have a chance of selection so a conclusion can be drawn about the whole population. Testing only items above a threshold is selective testing of specific items and provides no evidence about the untested remainder.

q: A key limitation of monetary unit sampling that the auditor must address separately is:
o: It cannot be used where the population exceeds 10000 separate items
It cannot be combined with stratification of the population at all
It requires the recorded amounts to follow a normal distribution
It is weak on understatement and skips zero and credit balances
why: MUS gives selection probability proportional to recorded amount, so items recorded at zero, omitted altogether, or with credit balances are effectively excluded, making it weak for understatement. Population size and distribution shape are not constraints on MUS.

q: The auditor discovers that the receivables listing used to select a sample excluded a branch ledger. The correct response is:
o: Treat the omission as an anomaly and continue with the existing sample
Project the sample misstatement rate onto the branch ledger balances
Treat the population as incomplete and reselect over the full listing
Increase the sample by the proportion the branch bears to the total
why: Sampling conclusions extend only to the population from which the sample was drawn, so an incomplete population invalidates the extrapolation. Simply scaling up the sample does not create evidence about a segment never eligible for selection.

q: Which of the following best distinguishes statistical from non-statistical sampling under SA 530?
o: Statistical sampling uses random selection and measures sampling risk
Statistical sampling always produces a smaller sample size than other methods
Statistical sampling removes the need for judgement in evaluating results
Non-statistical sampling does not permit projection of misstatements found
why: The defining features of statistical sampling are random selection and the use of probability theory to quantify sampling risk. Judgement is still required throughout, and non-statistical samples must also be projected to the population.

q: When performing a test of controls, the auditor finds the control was not performed for a two week period during which the responsible officer was on leave. This is best treated as:
o: An anomaly, since the absence of the officer was a one-off event
A deviation over that period, which may need separate evaluation
A non-sampling risk that calls for no further evaluation by the team
A scope limitation that requires a modified audit opinion in all cases
why: Where a control operated differently for an identifiable part of the period, that part is effectively a separate population and needs its own evaluation or alternative procedures. Labelling it an anomaly would wrongly ignore every transaction in the affected period.

q: In evaluating a substantive sample, the auditor computes projected misstatement using the ratio method. This method is MOST appropriate when:
o: Misstatement amounts bear no relation at all to the book values of items
Only a single misstatement has been found in the entire sample
The population is heavily stratified and has a certainty stratum
Misstatements are roughly proportional to the book values of items
why: The ratio approach scales the misstatement to book value, so it fits when errors are proportionate to size. Where errors are of similar absolute size regardless of item value, the difference method is the better estimator.

q: The auditor increases the assessed risk of material misstatement for the existence of receivables. Assuming other substantive procedures are unchanged, the effect on the sample size for positive confirmations is:
o: No change, since confirmation sample size depends only on the population size
A decrease, because higher risk shifts reliance towards analytical work
An increase, because lower acceptable detection risk demands more evidence
An increase, but only where the entity operates from several locations
why: Higher assessed risk means detection risk must be driven lower, which requires more evidence and therefore a larger sample. Higher risk does not justify shifting reliance onto analytics, which are less precise for existence at the item level.
